questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of a distributed version control system (DVCS) like Git?
options: A central server stores all code and clients only keep lightweight metadata pointers
It eliminates the need for branches by overwriting files immediately in real time
Source code is compiled directly on a central mainframe before distribution to developers
Every developer clone contains the entire project history and repository mirror locally
questions.explanation: In Git's distributed architecture, every local clone is a full repository backup containing complete commit history, enabling offline operations and decentralized workflows.

questions.question: What fundamental data structure does Git use internally to represent commit history and object relationships?
options: Singly Linked List with integer auto-incrementing IDs
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of cryptographically hashed objects
B+ Tree indexed table stored in SQLite
Circular FIFO buffer allocated in cache memory
questions.explanation: Git models commits, trees, and blobs as immutable objects in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), linked together by their SHA-1 cryptographic hashes.

questions.question: What scenario causes Git to enter a 'detached HEAD' state?
options: When the local hard drive runs out of disk space during a merge
When two developers commit simultaneously with identical timestamps
Checking out a specific commit SHA, tag, or remote branch directly rather than a local named branch
When the remote GitHub server fails to respond to SSH handshakes
questions.explanation: A detached HEAD occurs when HEAD points directly to a commit SHA rather than a branch ref. Commits made in this state can be lost if not attached to a named branch before switching away.

questions.question: What is stored inside the hidden .git folder in your project root?
options: The entire object database, commit history, refs, configuration, hooks, and staging index
The operating system virtual machine hypervisor configuration
Only compiled binary bytecode and node dependency caches
Temporary scratch files that can be deleted safely at any time
questions.explanation: The `.git` directory contains the complete Git repository engine—including refs, objects, index, config, and commit history.

questions.question: What distinguishes Git from Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) like SVN or TFS?
options: Git allows full offline commits, branching, and history inspection without connecting to a central server
Git does not support branching or merging workflows
Git requires constant 24/7 internet connectivity to record file changes
CVCS stores all repositories in local developer RAM while Git uses tape storage
questions.explanation: CVCS requires a continuous connection to a central server for commits and history queries, whereas Git performs virtually all operations locally and instantaneously.

questions.question: What metadata is permanently recorded inside a Git 'commit' object?
options: The full source code of the operating system and BIOS version
Tree hash, parent commit hash(es), author, committer, timestamps, and commit message
The user's GitHub billing account details
The IP addresses of all computers that downloaded the repository
questions.explanation: A commit object captures the top-level tree hash (snapshot of project files), parent commit SHA pointers, author/committer credentials, timestamps, and the log message.

questions.question: What state is a file in after it has been modified in the working directory but not yet staged?
options: Modified (Unstaged)
Committed
Staged
Untracked (New)
questions.explanation: A previously tracked file that contains local edits is in the 'Modified' (unstaged) state until `git add` moves it to the 'Staged' state.

questions.question: Why does Git store file changes as full snapshots rather than delta difference lists?
options: Because snapshots consume zero hard drive storage space
Because Git cannot compute differences between files
Because delta storage is forbidden by open-source licenses
Snapshots allow rapid branch switching and cryptographic integrity verification without recalculating deltas
questions.explanation: Git treats data as a stream of snapshots over time. While packfiles compress identical blobs later, the conceptual snapshot model makes checkouts and history traversal extremely fast.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to create a commit with an inline descriptive message?
options: git commit --message = "Descriptive commit message"
git record -msg "Descriptive commit message"
git commit -m "Descriptive commit message"
git save -m "Descriptive commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -m "message"` records a snapshot of the staged changes with the provided inline log message.

questions.question: How can you stage and commit all modified tracked files in a single shortcut command?
options: git push --commit "Commit message"
git add --commit "Commit message"
git commit -all -save "Commit message"
git commit -am "Commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -am "..."` automatically stages all tracked modified files (not untracked files) and commits them in a single step.

questions.question: Which command connects your local repository to a remote repository hosted on GitHub?
options: git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git remote set-url new https://github.com/user/repo.git
git connect origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git link --remote https://github.com/user/repo.git
questions.explanation: `git remote add <name> <url>` registers a new remote repository alias (conventionally named `origin`).

questions.question: Which command un-stages a file from the staging area while preserving your modifications in the working directory?
options: git delete --staged <file>
git remove --keep <file>
git revert --soft <file>
git restore --staged <file> (or git reset HEAD <file>)
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged <file>` removes the specified file from the staging area without discarding local modifications in your working directory.

questions.question: What command removes untracked files and directories from the working tree that are not ignored by .gitignore?
options: git clear -untracked
git purge --all
git rm --untracked
git clean -fd
questions.explanation: `git clean -f` forces the deletion of untracked files, and `-d` includes untracked directories.

questions.question: What does git clone <url> do when executed in an empty directory?
options: It deploys the application directly to a live web server
It downloads the remote repository, initializes .git, checks out the default branch, and configures origin
It creates a shallow zip archive without commit history
It copies code to the clipboard without saving files to disk
questions.explanation: `git clone` initializes a new local directory, copies the entire remote repository and history, sets up remote tracking branches, and checks out the default branch.

questions.question: What does git rm <file> do compared to deleting the file using standard OS commands?
options: It deletes the file from the filesystem and stages the deletion in Git index automatically
It deletes the file from remote GitHub but keeps it locally
It creates a backup copy of the file in the root directory
It encrypts the file so other developers cannot read it
questions.explanation: `git rm <file>` removes the file from both the working directory and stages the removal in the index, ready for the next commit.

questions.question: What is a branch in Git from an architectural standpoint?
options: A physical hardware partition on the developer's storage drive
A database table containing locked rows
A complete duplicate copy of all project files in a separate folder
A lightweight, movable pointer (40-byte file) referencing a specific commit SHA
questions.explanation: In Git, a branch is merely a lightweight pointer containing the 40-character SHA of its latest commit. Creating a branch is virtually instantaneous and consumes only 41 bytes.

questions.question: Which command lists all local and remote branches in the repository?
options: git list --branches
git view-branches -v
git branch -a
git branch --show-all-remotes
questions.explanation: `git branch -a` (all) lists both local branches and remote-tracking branches (prefixed with `remotes/origin/`).

questions.question: Under what exact condition does a Git merge conflict occur?
options: Whenever a merge involves more than 10 files simultaneously
Whenever code comments contain special punctuation characters
When developers commit from different operating systems (Windows vs macOS)
When two branches modify the exact same lines of the same file differently since their common ancestor
questions.explanation: Merge conflicts happen when Git encounters competing changes to the same lines of code in the same file and cannot automatically determine which version is correct.

questions.question: Which command aborts an ongoing merge and returns your working tree to the pre-merge state?
options: git stop-merge
git merge --abort
git rollback --merge
git merge --cancel
questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` halts the merge process and restores the working directory and HEAD to the state before `git merge` was executed.

questions.question: Which command force-deletes a local branch containing unmerged changes?
options: git branch -force-del <branch-name>
git branch --kill <branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>
git drop-branch <branch-name>
questions.explanation: `git branch -D` (uppercase, shortcut for `--delete --force`) deletes a branch regardless of its merge status.

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: git rebase deletes all commit messages permanently while git merge preserves them
git rebase is an irreversible command that destroys code
git merge preserves complete history with a merge commit; git rebase re-applies commits on top of another base, creating a linear history
git merge is only for local branches; git rebase is only for GitHub
questions.explanation: `git merge` creates a new merge commit combining two histories. `git rebase` moves the base of your feature branch to the tip of target branch, rewriting commit SHAs to produce a clean linear history.

questions.question: How do you re-apply your most recently stashed changes and remove them from the stash stack?
options: git stash pop
git stash apply --clean
git stash restore
git stash extract
questions.explanation: `git stash pop` applies the modifications from the top of the stash stack (`stash@{0}`) back to your working directory and removes them from the stash list.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick <commit-sha> do?
options: Applies the exact changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch onto your currently checked-out branch
Replaces the current branch with a random commit
Deletes a specific commit from history across all branches
Picks the top 5 highest rated commits on GitHub
questions.explanation: `git cherry-pick <commit-sha>` copies the diff of a specific existing commit and commits it cleanly onto the current branch as a new commit.

questions.question: In open-source workflows on GitHub, what is a 'Fork'?
options: A command that terminates a repository connection
A hardware server rack used to host Git repositories
A personal, independent copy of another user's repository hosted under your own GitHub account
A software tool used to split commit messages into multiple lines
questions.explanation: A Fork creates a distinct copy of an upstream repository under your GitHub account, allowing you to freely experiment and submit pull requests without write access to the original project.

questions.question: What role do Branch Protection Rules play on GitHub?
options: They restrict repository access to a single computer IP address
They automatically delete branches after 7 days of inactivity
They enforce safeguards such as requiring peer PR approvals, passing CI checks, and preventing direct force-pushes to main
They encrypt repository files using user passwords
questions.explanation: Branch protection rules protect critical branches (like `main`) by requiring code reviews, passing CI/CD status checks, preventing deletions, and blocking direct `git push --force`.

questions.question: Which merge strategy on GitHub combines all commits in a PR into a single unified commit on the target branch?
options: Squash and Merge
Standard Create Merge Commit
Direct Mirror Push
Rebase and Fast-Forward
questions.explanation: 'Squash and Merge' condenses all individual WIP commits from the feature branch into a single clean commit with a consolidated message on the base branch.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a README.md file in a GitHub repository?
options: It stores the billing history of the repository
It contains encrypted database passwords for production deployment
It instructs the Git compiler how to build binary executables
It serves as the landing page documentation explaining the project's purpose, setup instructions, usage, and architecture
questions.explanation: `README.md` is written in Markdown and renders automatically on the repository root page to guide developers on installation, prerequisites, and features.

questions.question: What does a 'Draft Pull Request' indicate on GitHub?
options: Work is in progress and open for discussion, but not yet ready for formal review or merging
The PR has been permanently rejected by the maintainers
The PR has failed automated unit test validation
The PR can only be viewed by GitHub employees
questions.explanation: Draft PRs allow developers to share work-in-progress code and trigger CI pipelines while signaling to the team that the branch is not yet ready for final review.

questions.question: How do you update an existing open Pull Request after making changes based on reviewer feedback?
options: Delete the remote branch and recreate it from scratch
Commit your changes locally and run git push origin <feature-branch>—the PR updates automatically
Close the current PR and open a brand new PR with the new code
Email the updated file attachments directly to the reviewer
questions.explanation: A Pull Request tracks the branch head. Pushing new commits to the remote feature branch automatically updates the PR diff, discussion timeline, and triggers CI checks.

questions.question: Which command generates a new high-security Ed25519 SSH key pair on your machine?
options: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
ssh-auth --generate-key ed25519
github-keys generate --email "..."
git create-ssh --type ed25519
questions.explanation: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "email"` generates a modern, cryptographically secure Ed25519 SSH public/private key pair.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a DNS (Domain Name System) server in web architecture?
options: Rendering DOM trees and executing JavaScript code on client machines
Storing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript source files directly on edge web servers
Translating human-readable domain names (e.g., example.com) into numerical IP addresses
Encrypting HTTP request payloads before transmission over the public Internet
questions.explanation: DNS acts as the Internet's address book, translating domain names like 'google.com' into machine-routable IP addresses like '142.250.190.46'.

questions.question: In the TCP 3-way handshake used to establish a reliable connection between client and server, what is the exact order of packet flags sent?
options: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
PING -> PONG -> ACK
ACK -> SYN -> SYN-ACK
SYN -> ACK -> FIN
questions.explanation: The TCP handshake begins with the client sending a SYN packet, the server replying with SYN-ACK, and the client confirming with an ACK packet before data transmission begins.

questions.question: Why is HTTP described as a 'stateless' protocol?
options: The protocol cannot send binary data such as images or video streams
Servers are legally prohibited from caching user data across sessions
Each request from a client is treated as completely independent, with the server retaining no memory of past requests by default
Clients must re-establish a brand new TCP connection for every single asset requested
questions.explanation: Statelessness means the server does not retain session context between transactions; state must be maintained explicitly using cookies, tokens, or sessions.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a Reverse Proxy (e.g., Nginx, HAProxy) in web architecture?
options: To inspect and filter outgoing traffic initiated by internal employees within a corporate intranet
To sit in front of web/application servers to handle load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and routing client requests
To compile JavaScript code into native machine code directly on client devices
To replace relational database storage engines with file system caches
questions.explanation: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers to intercept incoming client requests, performing load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and security filtering.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code series represents Client Errors, such as malformed requests, unauthorized access, or non-existent routes?
questions.explanation: 4xx status codes indicate client-side errors (e.g., 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found).

questions.question: In the URL 'https://api.example.com:8080/v1/users?role=admin#section2', which component represents the query parameters?
options: api.example.com
role=admin
#section2
questions.explanation: In a URL, the query string follows the '?' symbol (here 'role=admin'), while '#section2' is the fragment/hash identifier.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the difference between an Application Server (e.g., Gunicorn, Uvicorn, Node.js) and a Web Server (e.g., Nginx, Apache)?
options: There is no difference; both terms refer to the exact same software component
Web servers parse SQL queries directly, while application servers handle DNS routing
Application servers only run on mobile phones, whereas web servers only run in physical cloud datacenters
Web servers specialize in serving static files and routing traffic, whereas application servers execute dynamic server-side application logic and database interactions
questions.explanation: Web servers (Nginx/Apache) handle static files, SSL termination, and reverse proxy routing, while application servers execute dynamic programming logic (Python/Django/Node.js).

questions.question: What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) enforced by modern web browsers?
options: A rule that forces every web server to share its database credentials with clients
A network restriction preventing a computer from opening multiple browser tabs simultaneously
A core security mechanism that restricts scripts on one origin from accessing or reading sensitive DOM/data on a different origin (protocol, domain, or port mismatch)
A policy requiring all web pages to use the same CSS styling framework
questions.explanation: Same-Origin Policy isolates potentially malicious documents, preventing scripts on `site-a.com` from reading cookies or DOM data belonging to `site-b.com`.

questions.question: Which `<meta>` tag is essential inside `<head>` to ensure proper scaling and responsive rendering on mobile devices?
options: <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="mobile=1">
<meta name="responsive" content="true">
<meta name="screen-size" content="device-width">
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
questions.explanation: The viewport meta tag instructs mobile browsers to set the viewport width to the device screen width and establish an initial 1:1 zoom ratio.

questions.question: What is the primary semantic distinction between the `<article>` and `<section>` elements in HTML5?
options: `<article>` is meant for self-contained, independently distributable content (e.g., a blog post or tweet), whereas `<section>` groups thematic content typically with a heading
`<article>` can only contain plain text, whereas `<section>` can only contain images
`<article>` creates a sidebar layout, whereas `<section>` creates full-width containers
`<section>` is used exclusively for page headers, whereas `<article>` is used exclusively for footers
questions.explanation: An `<article>` represents an independent, reusable composition (like a blog post, comment, or product card), whereas a `<section>` represents a standalone generic section of a document grouped by theme.

questions.question: Which element pair is semantically designed to group an illustrative image or code snippet together with its descriptive caption?
options: and
<media> and <caption>
<figure> and <figcaption>
<picture> and <label>
questions.explanation: The `<figure>` element encapsulates self-contained content (like diagrams, photos, or code snippets), and `<figcaption>` provides its associated caption.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a correct, accessible HTML heading hierarchy structure?
questions.explanation: Headings must follow a logical sequential order without skipping levels downward (e.g., from `<h1>` directly to `<h4>`), allowing screen readers to construct a meaningful outline.

questions.question: What is the proper attribute syntax in HTML5 to store private custom data directly on an HTML element for JavaScript consumption?
options: custom-* (e.g., custom-user-id="42")
meta-* (e.g., meta-user-id="42")
data-* (e.g., data-user-id="42")
var-* (e.g., var-user-id="42")
questions.explanation: HTML5 specifies the `data-*` prefix for embedding custom data attributes on standard elements, accessible via JavaScript's `element.dataset` property.

questions.question: What does the `lang="en"` attribute on the root `<html>` element accomplish?
options: It restricts users from typing non-English characters into input forms
It sets the character encoding of the database server to English UTF-8
It automatically translates any foreign words on the webpage into English
It informs browsers, search engines, and screen readers of the primary natural language of the document for correct pronunciation and indexing
questions.explanation: The `lang` attribute declares the base natural language of the text, enabling screen readers to load correct pronunciation engines and assisting search engines.

questions.question: What is the semantic role of the `<time>` element in HTML5?
options: To pause JavaScript execution for a specified number of seconds
To measure the network latency and loading speed of the current webpage
To represent a specific period in time or a timestamp in a machine-readable format using the `datetime` attribute
To display an animated real-time countdown clock in the browser toolbar
questions.explanation: The `<time>` element represents time or date data, providing a machine-readable ISO format via the `datetime` attribute (e.g., `<time datetime="2026-09-11">`).

questions.question: Which `<form>` attribute specifies the MIME type encoding used when submitting forms containing binary files?
options: enctype="binary/octet-stream"
enctype="text/plain"
enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
enctype="multipart/form-data"
questions.explanation: When uploading files via `<input type="file">`, the form must use `method="POST"` and `enctype="multipart/form-data"` so the browser splits inputs into MIME parts.

questions.question: What happens when a form control has the `disabled` attribute compared to the `readonly` attribute upon form submission?
options: Both `disabled` and `readonly` fields are submitted normally with empty values
Fields with `readonly` are omitted from submission, while `disabled` fields are submitted
Fields with `disabled` are omitted from the form submission payload, while fields with `readonly` are included and sent
Neither `disabled` nor `readonly` fields can ever be inspected via JavaScript DOM
questions.explanation: A `disabled` input is ignored during form submission (not submitted in the payload), whereas a `readonly` input prevents user edits but submits its value.

questions.question: How do you group multiple radio buttons together so that selecting one automatically deselects the others?
options: Give all radio buttons in the group the exact same `name` attribute
Give all radio buttons the exact same `id` attribute
Wrap each radio button in the same `<fieldset>` without any names
Set their `type` attribute to `type="radio-group"`
questions.explanation: Radio buttons sharing the same `name` attribute belong to a mutual exclusion group where only one radio button can be checked at a time.

questions.question: Which HTML5 input type provides a slider control for selecting a numerical value within a bounded range?
options: <input type="number-bar">
<input type="scroll">
<input type="range">
<input type="slider">
questions.explanation: `<input type="range">` renders a slider control allowing the user to select an imprecise or bounded numeric value between `min` and `max`.

questions.question: Which HTML element is semantically designed to display the calculated result of a user action or form calculation?
options: <output>
<calc>
<computed>
<result>
questions.explanation: The `<output>` element represents the calculation result from script operations or form calculations (e.g., dynamic pricing or range sliders).

questions.question: Why is client-side HTML5 form validation alone never sufficient for web application security?
options: Modern web browsers charge licensing fees for verifying form constraints
HTML5 input validation only works when the client is disconnected from the Internet
Client-side validation causes severe memory leaks in the browser's DOM parser
Client-side validation can easily be bypassed, modified, or disabled by attackers using developer tools or direct API requests (e.g., curl/Postman)
questions.explanation: Client validation improves user experience, but server-side validation is strictly mandatory because anyone can send raw HTTP requests directly to backend endpoints.

questions.question: What autocomplete attribute value is recommended for password fields to assist password managers when a user registers a new account?
options: autocomplete="current-password"
autocomplete="generate"
autocomplete="new-password"
autocomplete="create-pass"
questions.explanation: `autocomplete="new-password"` prompts password managers to generate and store a secure strong password instead of autofilling existing credentials.

questions.question: What is the purpose of including a hidden input field (`<input type="hidden">`) with a CSRF token in server-rendered forms?
options: To compress images uploaded by the user before network transmission
To protect the application against Cross-Site Request Forgery by ensuring the form submission originated from an authenticated session on the trusted site
To bypass HTTPS encryption overhead on local development servers
To store the user's plain-text credit card number securely in the browser cache
questions.explanation: CSRF tokens stored in hidden inputs validate that the request was generated by the actual authenticated user and not forged by a malicious third-party site.

questions.question: Which HTML attribute is used to make a single table cell span across 3 columns horizontally?
options: span-col="3"
col-width="3"
rowspan="3"
colspan="3"
questions.explanation: `colspan="3"` causes a `<td>` or `<th>` cell to extend across 3 horizontal columns, while `rowspan` merges cells vertically across rows.

questions.question: What should the `alt` attribute contain for a purely decorative image that conveys no informative meaning (e.g., decorative divider lines)?
options: alt="null"
alt="decorative image"
alt="" (an empty alt attribute)
Omit the alt attribute completely from the tag
questions.explanation: An empty `alt=""` tells screen readers to ignore the decorative image completely. Omitting the `alt` tag entirely is an accessibility error that causes screen readers to announce the raw file URL.

questions.question: Which HTML5 element is specifically designed for 'Art Direction' and serving different image sources based on media query conditions?
options: <image-group> with CSS background rules
containing multiple elements and an fallback
<canvas> with WebGL responsive shaders
<svg-responsive> with embedded bitmaps
questions.explanation: The `` element wraps multiple `` tags alongside a fallback ``, allowing developers to serve different crops or formats (e.g., AVIF/WebP) per screen size.

questions.question: What does the `sandbox` attribute on an `<iframe>` element accomplish?
options: It limits the CPU and RAM allocation of the embedded page to exactly 10MB
It renders the embedded webpage in a high-contrast black-and-white theme
It forces the iframe to load only from localhost testing servers
It applies strict security restrictions (disabling scripts, popups, form submissions, and same-origin access) unless explicitly re-enabled with tokens
questions.explanation: The `sandbox` attribute heavily restricts untrusted third-party iframe content by disabling scripts, forms, popups, and same-origin cookies unless explicit exceptions like `allow-scripts` are added.

questions.question: What is the foundational 'First Rule of ARIA' in web development?
options: If you can use a native HTML5 element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require, use it instead of repurposing an element with ARIA
Every single `<div>` must have an ARIA landmark attribute attached
Always add `role="button"` to every `<button>` element to ensure full compatibility
ARIA attributes should only be written in uppercase letters
questions.explanation: The First Rule of ARIA states: If a native HTML element (like `<button>`, `<nav>`, `<dialog>`) already has built-in semantic behavior and keyboard support, never replace it with a `<div>` styled with ARIA roles.

questions.question: What is the accessibility impact of assigning `tabindex="0"` to a custom element (like a `<div>`)?
options: It forces the element to be the very first focused element when the page loads
It turns the element into an automatic submit button for forms
It inserts the element into the natural keyboard tab navigation order and makes it focusable via the Tab key
It permanently removes the element from keyboard navigation entirely
questions.explanation: `tabindex="0"` places an element into the sequential keyboard navigation flow. `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only via JavaScript, while positive tabindex values are discouraged as an anti-pattern.

questions.question: What is the purpose of providing a 'Skip to Content' link at the top of a webpage?
options: To load the page in low-bandwidth mode by omitting all images and videos
To allow keyboard-only and screen reader users to bypass repetitive header navigation menus and jump directly to main content
To close the current browser window quickly using keyboard shortcuts
To automatically skip past all paywalls on news subscription websites
questions.explanation: A skip link allows keyboard and screen reader users to jump over large navigation headers straight to `<main id="main-content">`, saving significant tabbing effort.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the 4-part specificity weight calculation for standard CSS selectors (Inline, ID, Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class, Element/Pseudo-element)?
options: Universal selector * (1,0,0,0) > ID (0,1,0,0) > Class (0,0,1,0) > Element (0,0,0,1)
Inline styles (1,0,0,0) > ID (#id: 0,1,0,0) > Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class (.class, [attr], :hover: 0,0,1,0) > Element/Pseudo-element (div, ::after: 0,0,0,1)
ID (1,0,0,0) > Inline styles (0,1,0,0) > Element (0,0,1,0) > Class (0,0,0,1)
questions.explanation: CSS Specificity is calculated as a 4-tier vector (a, b, c, d): Inline styles = (1,0,0,0), ID selectors = (0,1,0,0), Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes = (0,0,1,0), and Elements/Pseudo-elements = (0,0,0,1).

questions.question:
Which combinator selector matches only paragraphs (`

`) that are direct, immediate children of a `

` element?
options: div + p
div p
div > p
div ~ p
questions.explanation: The child combinator (`>`) targets direct children only, whereas the descendant combinator (space) targets all descendants regardless of nesting depth.

questions.question: Which attribute selector matches elements whose `href` attribute begins exactly with 'https://'?
options: a[href~="https://"]
a[href^="https://"]
a[href$="https://"]
a[href*="https://"]
questions.explanation: `^=` matches values that start with the specified string, `$=` matches values that end with the string, and `*=` matches substrings appearing anywhere.

questions.question: Which property is strictly required when declaring pseudo-elements `::before` or `::after` for them to render on the page?
options: visibility
position
content
display
questions.explanation: Pseudo-elements `::before` and `::after` will not render in the document tree unless the `content` property is explicitly defined (even as an empty string `content: '';`).

questions.question: Which of the following CSS properties is inherited by child elements by default?
options: padding
background-color
border
font-family
questions.explanation: Typography and textual properties (like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`) inherit automatically, while box model properties (`margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`) do not.

questions.question: How do you declare and access a CSS Custom Property (CSS variable) correctly?
options: Declare with `var:` prefix (e.g., `var:brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `#brand-blue;`
Declare with `$` prefix (e.g., `$brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `val($brand-blue);`
Declare with `--` prefix (e.g., `--brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `var(--brand-blue, #000);`
Declare with `@` prefix (e.g., `@brand-blue: #0070f3;`) and access using `get(@brand-blue);`
questions.explanation: CSS variables are defined on any selector (often `:root`) with a `--` prefix and retrieved using the `var(--custom-property-name, fallback)` function.

questions.question: What is the primary performance drawback of using `@import` inside a CSS file compared to `<link rel="stylesheet">` in HTML?
options: `@import` disables all JavaScript execution on modern mobile web browsers
`@import` creates sequential waterfall network requests by waiting for the parent stylesheet to download before initiating child downloads
`@import` converts CSS colors to low-resolution monochrome gradients
`@import` files are completely ignored by search engine indexing bots
questions.explanation: `<link>` tags allow browsers to discover and download stylesheets in parallel, whereas `@import` delays stylesheet downloads by creating a blocking sequential network waterfall.

questions.question: Why should the `!important` declaration be avoided in general CSS authoring whenever possible?
options: It incurs monetary server hosting charges for each page render
It prevents browsers from caching CSS files in local storage
It causes browser rendering engines to crash when compiling CSSOM trees
It breaks the natural cascading specificity hierarchy and makes debugging and overriding styles difficult in larger codebases
questions.explanation: `!important` overrides normal specificity rules, creating maintenance headaches because the only way to override an `!important` declaration is another `!important` with higher specificity.

questions.question: What is the effect of the `:focus-within` pseudo-class?
options: It prevents all child elements within a form from receiving focus
It targets only the very first `<input>` inside an active modal dialog
It matches an element if the element itself OR any of its descendant children currently has keyboard/mouse focus
It matches an input field only when the user is actively typing text inside it
questions.explanation: `:focus-within` allows styling a parent container (like highlighting a whole form group or navigation bar) when any child element inside it gains focus.

questions.question: What does the `&` symbol represent in modern native CSS Nesting?
options: A command that forces the browser to recompile CSS into WebAssembly
A logical AND operator that requires two stylesheets to load simultaneously
An escape character used for unicode typography symbols
A nesting selector that explicitly references and represents the parent selector rule
questions.explanation: In modern native CSS nesting, `&` represents the parent selector, allowing modifier classes (e.g., `&.is-open`) and pseudo-classes (e.g., `&:hover`) to be nested cleanly.

questions.question: Under the standard default CSS box model (`box-sizing: content-box`), if an element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px`, `border: 5px solid black`, and `margin: 15px`, what is its total rendered horizontal space on the page?
options: 200px total occupied space
240px total occupied space
280px total occupied space (Content 200 + Padding Left/Right 40 + Border Left/Right 10 + Margin Left/Right 30)
250px total occupied space
questions.explanation: Under `content-box`, total horizontal space = Content (200px) + Padding (20px * 2 = 40px) + Border (5px * 2 = 10px) + Margin (15px * 2 = 30px) = 280px. Total element width is 250px.

questions.question: What is the standard CSS universal reset snippet used by modern developers to enforce consistent border-box sizing across all elements and pseudo-elements?
options: html { border-box: true; }
body { box-sizing: all; }
:root { sizing: border-box !default; }
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
questions.explanation: Targeting `*`, `*::before`, and `*::after` ensures every element and generated pseudo-element adheres to predictable `border-box` calculations.

questions.question: Under what condition will `margin: 0 auto;` successfully center an element horizontally inside its parent container?
options: The element must have `display: inline` and no explicit width defined
The element must have `position: absolute` with `left: 0`
The element must be a block-level container with a specified, constrained `width` (or `max-width`) less than its parent
The parent container must have `overflow: scroll` enabled
questions.explanation: `margin: 0 auto` divides remaining horizontal space equally between left and right margins, which only works if the block element has an explicit width less than 100%.

questions.question: What is the key visual and layout difference between `outline` and `border` in CSS?
options: `outline` increases the total computed width of the element in the DOM
`outline` is only supported on SVG elements, whereas `border` is for HTML
`border` cannot have custom colors, whereas `outline` supports gradients
`outline` is drawn outside the element's border box and does NOT occupy space in the layout flow, so toggling it never causes content layout reflow
questions.explanation: Unlike `border`, an `outline` does not take up box model space or affect element dimensions, making it ideal for focus indicators without triggering layout shifts.

questions.question: How does `display: inline-block` differ from `display: inline`?
options: `inline-block` allows setting explicit `width`, `height`, and respects top/bottom margins and padding while still sitting inline on the same line with adjacent content
`inline-block` forces the element onto its own brand new line like a `<div>`
`inline-block` is deprecated and behaves identically to `display: none`
`inline-block` disables all background colors and text decoration styling
questions.explanation: `inline-block` elements flow inline horizontally like text, but gain full box model capabilities (explicit `width`, `height`, `margin-top/bottom`, `padding-top/bottom`).

questions.question: What is the difference between `em` and `rem` units in CSS sizing?
options: `rem` is always relative to the root `<html>` font size, whereas `em` is relative to the immediate parent element's font size (which can compound with nesting)
`em` is relative to root font size, while `rem` is relative to viewport height
`rem` only applies to margins, while `em` only applies to font sizes
`em` is fixed to 16px forever, while `rem` changes based on device screen resolution
questions.explanation: `rem` (Root EM) scales consistently relative to the root `<html>` element (default 16px), preventing the nested compounding issue seen with `em` units.

questions.question: What is the effect of applying a negative margin, such as `margin-top: -20px;`, to an element?
options: It pulls the element 20px upward, overlapping any content situated above it in the layout flow
It collapses the height of the element to zero pixels
It creates 20px of transparent white empty space above the element
It rotates the element 180 degrees vertically
questions.explanation: Negative margins pull the element in the direction of the negative value (or pull subsequent siblings toward itself if applied to bottom/right), allowing deliberate overlapping layouts.

questions.question: How do you create a perfect circle from a square element of `width: 100px; height: 100px;` using CSS?
options: clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 100%);
border-radius: 50%;
shape-outside: circle(100%);
border-radius: 100px 0 100px 0;
questions.explanation: Setting `border-radius: 50%` curves each corner by half the element's dimension, turning equal width and height squares into perfect circles.

questions.question: How does the CSS `clamp()` function work for responsive dimensions (e.g., `width: clamp(300px, 50vw, 800px);`)?
options: It sets a preferred value (`50vw`) that can scale dynamically, but guarantees the value will never drop below `300px` or exceed `800px`
It restricts the element's width to exactly 300px on mobile and 800px on tablet
It calculates the average of the three numbers and sets a fixed pixel width
It rotates through the three values at 1-second animation intervals
questions.explanation: `clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)` clamps a scalable value between an absolute minimum floor and maximum ceiling, eliminating messy media query breakpoints.

questions.question: Which CSS mathematical function allows combining different measurement units in a single calculation (e.g., subtracting a fixed pixel sidebar from a percentage width)?
options: eval()
sum()
calc() (e.g., width: calc(100% - 250px);)
compute()
questions.explanation: The `calc()` function performs dynamic mathematical operations across mixed units, such as subtracting fixed pixel dimensions (`250px`) from relative percentages (`100%`).

questions.question: What is the key difference between setting opacity via `opacity: 0.5` versus setting a semi-transparent background via `background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)`?
options: `opacity: 0.5` only affects text color, leaving backgrounds fully opaque
`rgba()` disables all mouse click events on the element, while `opacity` does not
`opacity: 0.5` makes the target element AND all of its nested child elements semi-transparent, whereas `rgba()` only makes the background color semi-transparent
There is no difference; modern browsers treat them as identical rendering commands
questions.explanation: The `opacity` property affects the entire rendered stacking context including all child text and icons, whereas `rgba()` or `hsla()` only applies alpha transparency to the specific color property.

questions.question: Why is it considered a best practice to define a 'fallback font stack' (e.g., `font-family: 'Inter', Roboto, -apple-system, sans-serif;`)?
options: It allows the browser to download all four fonts simultaneously to increase rendering speed
If the user's browser fails to load or find the custom primary font, it gracefully falls back to available local system fonts rather than rendering broken characters
It is required by web hosting servers to validate font licensing certificates
It enables multiple languages to display simultaneously inside the same sentence
questions.explanation: A font stack provides an ordered fallback list; if the primary web font fails to load or is unavailable, the browser renders the next available system font.

questions.question: Why is setting a unitless `line-height` (e.g., `line-height: 1.5;`) strongly recommended over fixed pixel values (e.g., `line-height: 24px;`) on container elements?
options: Fixed pixel line-heights are completely ignored by modern mobile web browsers
Unitless line-height forces all paragraphs to take up exactly 100% of the viewport height
Unitless line-height converts all lowercase text to capital letters
Unitless `line-height` scales proportionally relative to each child element's individual `font-size`, preventing text collisions when children have larger headings
questions.explanation: When `line-height: 1.5` is inherited, child elements multiply 1.5 by their own font size. A fixed pixel value (e.g., `24px`) inherited by a `36px` heading causes text lines to overlap disastrously.

questions.question: Which CSS property creates a fixed 'Parallax' background effect where the background image stays stationary in the viewport while the rest of the page scrolls over it?
options: background-clip: viewport;
background-position: sticky;
background-attachment: fixed;
background-repeat: static;
questions.explanation: `background-attachment: fixed` fixes the background relative to the viewport, creating a classic parallax scrolling effect as content scrolls over the stationary image.

questions.question: What CSS standard property controls whether the browser can break words across lines in order to prevent long words or URLs from overflowing its container?
options: hyphen-mode: auto;
overflow-wrap: break-word; (or word-break: break-all;)
text-wrap: force;
letter-spacing: compress;
questions.explanation: `overflow-wrap: break-word` (formerly `word-wrap`) allows unbroken strings like long URLs to break onto new lines when they would otherwise overflow their containing box.

questions.question: How are multiple background image layers stacked when defined in a single `background` property (e.g., `background: url(top.png), url(bottom.png);`)?
options: The browser blends all layers equally into a single 50% opacity composite
Only the largest file size image is displayed; the other is ignored
The first background image listed is rendered on top (closest to the user), with subsequent layers rendered underneath in descending order
The last background image listed is rendered on top
questions.explanation: Multiple backgrounds are layered from front to back: the first image listed in the comma-separated CSS rule appears on top, closest to the viewer.

questions.question: Which CSS property removes the default underline from hyperlinks (`<a>` tags)?
options: text-decoration: none;
text-underline: hidden;
font-decoration: remove;
link-style: plain;
questions.explanation: `text-decoration: none` removes typographic underlines, overlines, or line-through strokes from text elements.

questions.question: What does the `text-transform: capitalize;` property do to text?
options: It capitalizes only the very first letter of the entire paragraph sentence
It converts the entire string into all capital uppercase letters
It converts the first letter of every individual word to uppercase while preserving the rest of the letters
It underlines all uppercase acronyms automatically
questions.explanation: `text-transform: capitalize` capitalizes the first character of each word, `uppercase` capitalizes every character, and `lowercase` makes all characters lowercase.

questions.question: How do you apply a multi-line text truncation to clamp a paragraph to exactly 3 visible lines with an ellipsis?
options: max-lines: 3; truncate: multi-line;
line-height: clamp(3); overflow: ellipsis;
display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden;
text-lines: 3; text-overflow: ellipsis; overflow: clip;
questions.explanation: Multi-line clamping is achieved via WebKit box properties: `display: -webkit-box`, `-webkit-line-clamp: 3`, `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`, and `overflow: hidden`.

questions.question: Which `background-clip` value allows text to take on the gradient color of the background image underneath it?
options: background-clip: text; (combined with color: transparent;)
background-clip: content-box;
background-clip: font-mask;
background-clip: border-box;
questions.explanation: `background-clip: text` (often `-webkit-background-clip: text`) clips the background graphic to the text character shapes, which when paired with `color: transparent` creates gradient text.

questions.question: In CSS Flexbox, which property determines whether the main axis runs horizontally or vertically?
options: flex-wrap
flex-direction
justify-content
align-items
questions.explanation: `flex-direction` establishes the main axis: `row`/`row-reverse` sets a horizontal main axis, while `column`/`column-reverse` sets a vertical main axis.

questions.question: What is the default value of the `align-items` property on a flex container?
options: center
flex-start
baseline
stretch
questions.explanation: By default, `align-items: stretch` causes flex items to expand along the cross axis to fill the full height (or width in column mode) of the flex container.

questions.question: What is the full expansion of the shorthand rule `flex: 1;`?
options: flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 0; flex-basis: auto;
flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%;
flex-grow: 0; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 100px;
flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: auto;
questions.explanation: The shorthand `flex: 1` expands to `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%`, making all items sharing `flex: 1` grow and shrink equally from a base of zero.

questions.question: Why do long unbroken strings or text elements sometimes cause flex items to overflow their container despite having `flex: 1` or `flex-shrink: 1`?
options: Browsers disable flex shrinking whenever fonts larger than 14px are rendered
Flexbox engines automatically convert overflowing text into base64 images
Flex items have a default `min-width: auto;` (minimum content size), which prevents them from shrinking smaller than their inner content width
`flex-shrink` only applies to images and disallows text shrinking
questions.explanation: In Flexbox, items default to `min-width: auto`, meaning the browser won't shrink an item below its content width. Setting `min-width: 0;` on the flex item resolves the overflow issue.

questions.question: How do you achieve perfect horizontal and vertical centering of a child element inside a flex container?
options: display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;
display: flex; flex-direction: center; margin: 0 auto;
display: flex; align-content: center; text-align: center;
display: flex; justify-items: center; align-self: center;
questions.explanation: Setting `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;` centers children along both the main axis and cross axis simultaneously.

questions.question: When `flex-direction: column` is declared, how do the alignment properties change their axes?
options: All alignment properties are disabled in column mode
`justify-content` controls horizontal alignment, and `align-items` controls vertical alignment
Both `justify-content` and `align-items` control vertical alignment simultaneously
`justify-content` controls vertical alignment (main axis), and `align-items` controls horizontal alignment (cross axis)
questions.explanation: Changing `flex-direction` to `column` rotates the main axis vertically (Y-axis) and the cross axis horizontally (X-axis), swapping the directional impact of `justify-content` and `align-items`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `flex: auto;` and `flex: none;`?
options: `flex: auto` calculates width based on the user's internet speed
`flex: none` hides all flex items from the screen using `visibility: hidden`
`flex: auto` (`1 1 auto`) allows items to grow and shrink based on their size, while `flex: none` (`0 0 auto`) makes items completely rigid and non-flexible
`flex: none` resets all children to standard CSS table cells
questions.explanation: `flex: none` expands to `0 0 auto` (cannot grow, cannot shrink, sized by width/height/content), whereas `flex: auto` expands to `1 1 auto` (fully flexible).

questions.question: What happens to text nodes directly inside a flex container that are not wrapped in an HTML tag?
options: The browser wraps them in an anonymous flex item that participates fully in flex formatting rules
The browser deletes the text nodes during CSSOM compilation
The text nodes escape the flex container and render at the bottom of the `<body>`
The browser displays a console syntax error and stops rendering
questions.explanation: Raw text inside a flex container is automatically encapsulated within an anonymous flex item and sized/aligned according to flex rules.

questions.question: What does the fractional unit `1fr` represent in CSS Grid?
options: One share of the remaining available free space in the grid container after fixed tracks are allocated
One fraction of the root font size (equivalent to 16px)
Exactly 100% of the viewport width on full-screen monitors
A fixed measurement equivalent to 1 frame per second animation speed
questions.explanation: The `fr` (fractional) unit divides available remaining space proportionally among tracks after accounting for fixed pixel/content dimensions and gaps.

questions.question: How do you define visual ASCII layout areas in CSS Grid using `grid-template-areas`?
options: grid-template-areas: [header, sidebar, main, footer];
grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer";
grid-template-areas: layout { header; sidebar; main; footer; };
grid-template-areas: area(header) -> area(main) -> area(footer);
questions.explanation: `grid-template-areas` defines named grid cells visually as quoted strings representing rows, mapped to child items using `grid-area: header;`.

questions.question: What does the line shorthand `grid-column: 1 / 4;` mean for a grid item?
options: The item is visible only on January 4th in calendar widgets
The item starts at grid line 1 and spans across to grid line 4 (covering 3 columns)
The item is placed in row 1, column 4 as a single cell
The item takes up 1/4th (25%) of the total container height
questions.explanation: `grid-column: 1 / 4` specifies `grid-column-start: 1` and `grid-column-end: 4`, spanning 3 grid column tracks across lines 1, 2, 3, and 4.

questions.question: What does the `subgrid` feature (`grid-template-columns: subgrid;`) allow a nested child grid to do?
options: Limit the nested grid to exactly 2 columns on all devices
Automatically convert all grid items into an SVG vector canvas
Inherit and align directly to the grid tracks and line definitions of its parent grid container
Create a separate 3D WebGL coordinate space inside the grid cell
questions.explanation: `subgrid` allows child grid containers to share the track sizing and alignment of their parent grid, ensuring nested elements (like card headers or footers) align across sibling cards.

questions.question: How can two distinct grid items be made to overlap in CSS Grid without using `position: absolute`?
options: Assign both items to the same overlapping grid row and column coordinates (e.g., both having `grid-area: 1 / 1 / 3 / 3;`) and adjust layering with `z-index`
Set `grid-overlap: enable;` on the parent container
Overlap is impossible in CSS Grid without absolute positioning
Give both elements a negative `grid-gap` value
questions.explanation: Grid items can share identical grid lines or overlapping areas naturally; normal stacking rules and `z-index` dictate which overlapping item renders on top.

questions.question: Which CSS Multi-column property controls how many vertical newspaper-style columns a block of text splits into?
options: grid-template-columns
column-count
column-divisions
text-columns
questions.explanation: The CSS Multi-column Layout property `column-count` defines the exact number of columns text flows through in newspaper style.

questions.question: What is the effect of using negative grid line indices (e.g., `grid-column: 1 / -1;`)?
options: `-1` rotates the grid item 180 degrees backwards
`-1` hides the grid item behind the background layer
`-1` references the very last explicit grid line on the opposite edge, allowing an item to span the full width of the explicit grid
`-1` throws a CSS validation error because line numbers must be positive integers
questions.explanation: Negative line numbers count backward from the end of the explicit grid: line `-1` is the last line, `-2` is the second to last line, etc.

questions.question: What is the default value of the CSS `position` property on HTML elements?
options: relative
absolute
initial-flow
static
questions.explanation: By default, elements have `position: static`, meaning they participate in normal document flow and ignore `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, and `z-index`.

questions.question: What serves as the 'Containing Block' for an element with `position: absolute;`?
options: The immediate parent element regardless of its CSS positioning property
The nearest ancestor element that has a `position` property other than `static` (e.g., `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`)
Always the top-level `<body>` element regardless of parent styles
The nearest element that has `display: flex` or `display: grid`
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element searches up the DOM tree for the nearest ancestor with `position` set to anything other than `static`. If none exists, it falls back to the Initial Containing Block (viewport).

questions.question: What is the key characteristic of an element with `position: fixed`?
options: It is removed from normal flow and positioned relative to the viewport, remaining in the exact same screen position when the page scrolls
It locks into position only after scrolling 500px down the page
It expands to cover 100% of the screen height automatically
It cannot contain any clickable links or form buttons
questions.explanation: `position: fixed` fixes an element relative to the browser viewport coordinate space, remaining pinned on screen during scrolling.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common reason why `position: sticky; top: 0;` fails to stick when scrolling?
options: The viewport width is greater than 1200px
An ancestor element in the DOM tree has `overflow: hidden`, `overflow: auto`, or `overflow: scroll` applied
The webpage uses HTML5 semantic tags instead of `<div>` tags
The sticky element has a background color defined in hex format
questions.explanation: Any ancestor with `overflow: hidden`, `auto`, or `scroll` breaks `position: sticky` because the scroll context is trapped inside that parent rather than the main document viewport.

questions.question: Why can't a modal dialog with `z-index: 9999` appear above an element in another container if that modal's parent container has `z-index: 1` and the other element's parent has `z-index: 2`?
options: `z-index` values cannot exceed 1000 in modern web browsers
The browser rounds all z-index numbers down to zero upon page load
Modal dialogs are automatically rendered below all standard HTML text
Because the modal is trapped inside its parent's Stacking Context, and the entire parent context is subordinate to the higher `z-index: 2` context
questions.explanation: Stacking contexts form isolated hierarchies. A child's `z-index` only has meaning within its parent stacking context; it can never escape to out-stack a higher sibling stacking context.

questions.question: When percentage values are used on `top`, `bottom`, `left`, and `right` on an absolutely positioned element, what are they calculated relative to?
options: The physical diagonal resolution of the user's monitor
The width and height of the absolutely positioned element itself
The total height of the document body including off-screen scroll area
The width and height of the element's positioned Containing Block (padding box)
questions.explanation: Percentage offsets on positioned elements (`top/bottom: %`, `left/right: %`) resolve relative to the padding box dimensions of the containing block.

questions.question: Which of the following creates a new Stacking Context in modern CSS?
options: An element with `opacity: 0.95` (any opacity value strictly less than 1)
An element with `display: block` and `margin: 10px`
An element with `text-align: center`
An element with `font-weight: bold`
questions.explanation: Creating a stacking context happens via properties like `opacity < 1`, `transform != none`, `filter != none`, `position: relative/absolute with z-index != auto`, and `isolation: isolate`.

questions.question: What is the stacking behavior of two unpositioned (`position: static`) sibling elements without any z-index?
options: Unpositioned elements can never visually overlap under any circumstances
The element that appears later in the HTML source code renders on top of the earlier element if they overlap
The element with the larger file size renders on top
The earlier element in the HTML source code always renders on top
questions.explanation: In default document stacking, when elements occupy the same space without custom stacking contexts, later elements in source order stack on top of earlier siblings.

questions.question: What is the primary philosophy behind 'Mobile-First' responsive CSS design?
options: Creating two completely separate domain websites (e.g., m.example.com and www.example.com)
Building desktop layouts first, then using `max-width` media queries to hide elements on mobile
Writing base styles for small screens first, then using `min-width` media queries to progressively enhance the layout for larger screens
Disabling all CSS animations on mobile devices permanently
questions.explanation: Mobile-first design establishes lightweight baseline styling for mobile viewports, using `@media (min-width: ...)` queries to add complexity as screen real estate increases.

questions.question: Why should developers use `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` in modern web applications?
options: To accelerate video playback speed to 2x by default
To improve CPU battery life by automatically pausing background music
To compress GIF animations into WebP format on mobile
To minimize or eliminate non-essential animations and transitions for users with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity
questions.explanation: `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` respects user accessibility preferences by turning off jarring transitions and parallax effects that trigger motion sickness.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between CSS Container Queries (`@container`) and standard Media Queries (`@media`)?
options: Container Queries are deprecated in favor of CSS Flexbox
Media Queries query the dimensions of the entire browser viewport, whereas Container Queries query the size of an individual component's parent container
Media Queries can only resize text, while Container Queries can only resize images
Container Queries only work on Docker container server backends
questions.explanation: Container Queries allow a component (like a card) to adapt based on the width of its parent wrapper rather than the whole screen width, unlocking true modular UI components.

questions.question: Which media type query is used to format pages specifically for paper printing or PDF export (e.g., hiding navigation bars and changing background colors)?
options: @media export-pdf
@media print
@media paper
@media physical
questions.explanation: `@media print` targets print previews and printer output, allowing developers to hide navbars, force black text on white backgrounds, and control page breaks.

questions.question: In standard responsive UI design, what is a 'Breakpoint'?
options: A JavaScript error that pauses browser script execution
A specific viewport width threshold (e.g., 640px, 768px, 1024px) at which the page layout transitions using media queries
An HTML tag that forces a line break inside a paragraph
The point where an image file size exceeds the network bandwidth limit
questions.explanation: A breakpoint is the viewport width where media queries trigger layout modifications (e.g., switching from single-column mobile to multi-column desktop).

questions.question: Which media query detects whether a user's device has a high pixel density screen (such as Apple Retina displays)?
options: @media (gpu-render: retina)
@media (pixel-density: ultra)
@media (screen-quality: 4k)
@media (-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio: 2), (min-resolution: 192dpi)
questions.explanation: `min-resolution: 192dpi` (or `-webkit-min-device-pixel-ratio: 2`) targets high-density Retina screens to serve 2x high-resolution bitmap assets.

questions.question: Which media feature query detects if a user has requested high contrast in their system accessibility settings?
options: @media (prefers-contrast: more)
@media (contrast-mode: high)
@media (accessibility: max-contrast)
@media (high-contrast: active)
questions.explanation: `@media (prefers-contrast: more)` allows developers to enhance border outlines, increase font weights, and boost color contrast for visually impaired users.

questions.question: What was one of the most notable architectural changes introduced in Bootstrap 5 compared to Bootstrap 4?
options: Replacing all HTML5 tags with React JSX components
Completely dropping the jQuery dependency in favor of modern vanilla JavaScript
Removing the 12-column grid system in favor of table layouts
Requiring all stylesheets to be written in Python
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 eliminated the dependency on jQuery, rewritten completely in native vanilla JavaScript with improved performance and smaller bundle sizes.

questions.question: What are the 6 standard responsive breakpoint tiers in Bootstrap 5?
options: mobile (<480px), tablet (≥480px), desktop (≥1024px), ultra (≥2048px)
questions.explanation: Bootstrap 5 features 6 responsive tiers: `xs` (default <576px), `sm` (576px), `md` (768px), `lg` (992px), `xl` (1200px), and the new `xxl` (1400px).

questions.question: How do you create a column layout that stacks vertically as 100% width on mobile screens, splits into 2 equal columns on tablets (≥768px), and 4 equal columns on desktops (≥992px)?
options: col-1 col-md-2 col-lg-4
col-xs-12 col-tab-6 col-desk-4
col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-3
col-full col-tablet-half col-desktop-quarter
questions.explanation: In a 12-column grid: `col-12` = 100% width, `col-md-6` = 6/12 (50% or 2 per row), and `col-lg-3` = 3/12 (25% or 4 per row).

questions.question: Which utility class is used to shift a column 3 grid columns to the right on medium screens (≥768px)?
options: offset-md-3
col-skip-3
push-md-3
shift-md-3
questions.explanation: `.offset-md-3` applies `margin-left: 25%` (3/12 columns) at the `md` breakpoint to offset the column horizontally.

questions.question: What does the shorthand class `.row-cols-md-3` placed on a `.row` accomplish?
options: It sets the font size to 3rem across the entire row
It limits the maximum number of items in the database to 3
It automatically formats all immediate child `.col` elements into 3 equal columns per row on medium screens (≥768px) without needing `col-md-4` on every child
It creates exactly 3 empty rows in the DOM tree
questions.explanation: `.row-cols-*` sets how many columns appear per row at the container level, dynamically wrapping children into rows of 3 on `md` screens.

questions.question: How do you hide an element on mobile screens (<768px) and display it as a flexbox container on tablets and desktops (≥768px) using Bootstrap 5 utility classes?

hidden-xs flex-md
d-none d-md-flex

It applies a large border-radius (50rem) to create fully rounded stadium/pill shaped ends

questions.question: What does the `.text-truncate` class do when applied to a block element with a constrained width?

It hides the entire paragraph from the screen
It shrinks the font size to 8px automatically
It prevents text wrapping and truncates overflowing text with an ellipsis (`...`)

questions.question: How do you apply a 50% transparent dark background color to a container using Bootstrap 5 utility classes?

bg-dark-50

questions.question: What class is used to float an element to the right in Bootstrap 5 (supporting LTR and RTL directions)?

align-right
float-right
float-end

questions.question: What is the role of the `.navbar-toggler` button in a Bootstrap 5 navigation bar?
options: It submits the navigation search form to the backend server
It acts as the hamburger toggle button that expands or collapses the mobile navigation menu via `data-bs-toggle="collapse"`
It toggles between dark mode and light mode themes
It rotates the brand logo 360 degrees

questions.question: What is the standard HTML structure for a basic Bootstrap 5 Card component?

`.card` > `<header>` > `<main>` > `<footer>`
`.card` > `.card-row` > `.card-column`
`.card` > optional `.card-header` + `.card-body` (containing `.card-title` and `.card-text`) + optional `.card-footer`

questions.question: How do you prevent a Bootstrap 5 Modal from closing when a user clicks outside the modal dialog backdrop?

Set `modal-dismiss: none;` in CSS
Add `data-bs-close="false"` to the modal
Add `data-bs-backdrop="static"` to the modal container

questions.question: How do you activate native Bootstrap 5 client-side form validation styles upon form submission?

Add the `.was-validated` class to the `<form class="needs-validation">` container via JavaScript
Call `form.submitBootstrapValidation()` in JavaScript

questions.question: What is the Offcanvas component in Bootstrap 5 primarily used for?

Exporting HTML tables directly to Microsoft Excel spreadsheets
Rendering 3D graphic animations using WebGL canvas

questions.question: Which class turns a checkbox into a modern iOS-style toggle switch in Bootstrap 5?

.form-check.form-switch (wrapping `<input type="checkbox" class="form-check-input">`)
.form-toggle
.switch-control

questions.question: What class makes a Bootstrap 5 Alert dismissible with a functional close button (`.btn-close`)?

alert alert-cancel

questions.question: What class is used to center a modal vertically on the screen rather than pinning it to the top?
options: modal-align-middle
modal-vertical-center
modal-dialog-centered
modal-center

questions.question: Which class enables smooth horizontal scrolling within a table that overflows narrow viewports?

table-fluid
table-overflow
table-scroll

questions.question: Which class makes a group of cards in a grid maintain identical uniform heights?

card-equal
card-same-height

questions.question: How do you enable Dark Mode globally across an entire website in Bootstrap 5.3+?

Add `data-bs-theme="dark"` to the root `<html>` element

Add the class `.dark-mode-all` to the `<body>` element

questions.question: What is the primary recommended approach for deeply customizing Bootstrap themes, colors, and typography for enterprise applications?
options: Using JavaScript `element.style` modifications on every DOM node
Directly modifying the minified `bootstrap.min.css` file in `node_modules`
Customizing Bootstrap Sass source files (`.scss`) by overriding `$theme-colors` and default variables before compiling to CSS
Writing thousands of `!important` rules in a separate override CSS file

questions.question: How do you add a custom theme color (e.g., 'accent': #e11d48) to Bootstrap's `$theme-colors` map in Sass?

$theme-colors: ("accent": #e11d48); @import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap";

questions.question: What is the purpose of using a tool like PurgeCSS or UnCSS in a production build pipeline with Bootstrap?

To generate automatic dark mode images
To convert all CSS into WebAssembly machine code
To analyze HTML/JS files and remove unused Bootstrap CSS classes, shrinking production CSS bundle size by up to 80-90%

questions.question: How can you reduce the CSS bundle size when importing Bootstrap using Sass?
options: Disable CSS Grid inside the browser developer settings

Change the file extension from `.scss` to `.txt`
Import only the specific component Sass partials needed (e.g., `@import "bootstrap/scss/buttons";`) instead of `@import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap";`
questions.explanation: Modular Sass imports allow developers to bundle only required components (grid, buttons, navbar), eliminating unused components from the final CSS bundle.

questions.question: How do you enable Right-to-Left (RTL) text direction support in Bootstrap 5 for languages like Arabic or Hebrew?

Add `text-direction: reverse;` to all paragraph tags
Add `dir="rtl"` to `<html>` and include the RTLCSS compiled stylesheet (`bootstrap.rtl.min.css`)

questions.question: How do you customize the focus ring color on form inputs using Bootstrap Sass variables?

questions.question: How can you scope Bootstrap 5 styles to a specific container (e.g., `#my-widget`) to prevent style leaks in a microfrontend application?

Bootstrap styles cannot be scoped under any circumstances
Add `scoped="true"` to the `<link>` tag in HTML
Rename all Bootstrap classes with a random hash suffix manually

questions.question: How do you override a component-specific CSS variable for just one individual button without affecting other buttons?

Apply custom inline CSS or a modifier class (e.g., `.btn-custom { --bs-btn-padding-y: 1.2rem; --bs-btn-bg: #8b5cf6; }`)
Delete the Bootstrap button stylesheet from the server
questions.explanation: Component-scoped CSS variables allow targeting single instances (e.g., `.btn-hero { --bs-btn-bg: #8b5cf6; }`) without affecting global button styles.

questions.question: Which Bootstrap 5 Sass variable controls the default body font family across the entire framework?
options: $font-family-base
$typography-primary
$global-font
$body-font
